date.note: Dating is debated. Michael Lecker treats the document as a single legal framework drawn up shortly after the emigration of 1/622. Muhammad Hamidullah held that its first part (on the Emigrants and Helpers) belongs to the first year after the Hijra and suggested that its code for the Jews was added after the Battle of Badr (2/624). R. B. Serjeant divided it into eight separate documents issued over several years of the Medinan period. Fred Donner notes that the document's silence on the three main Jewish clans has been read by some as a sign of a later date. The year given is the earliest proposed and is approximate.

summary: The Constitution of Medina is a document attributed to Muhammad, preserved in Ibn Ishaq's biography and in Abu Ubayd's Kitab al-Amwal, that sets out mutual obligations among the Meccan Emigrants, the Medinan Helpers, and some of the Jewish groups of Yathrib. Most modern scholars accept it as an early and substantially authentic text, while its unity, date, and the identity of its Jewish parties remain debated.
description:
The Constitution of Medina, also called the Sahifa ('document'), the umma document, or simply the Kitab, is a text presented as 'a document from Muhammad the prophet' governing relations 'between the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib, and those who followed them and joined them and laboured with them'. The original is lost; its text survives, with mostly minor variations, in two early literary works, the biography of Muhammad by Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767) in the recension of Ibn Hisham, and the Kitab al-Amwal of Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam (d. 224/838). Ibn Ishaq introduces it as a document in which Muhammad 'made a friendly agreement with the Jews and established them in their religion and their property, and stated the reciprocal obligations'.

In Guillaume's translation of Ibn Ishaq, the text declares the believers 'one community (umma) to the exclusion of all men'. It provides that the Emigrants of Quraysh and each of the Medinan clans shall pay blood-money and ransom their prisoners according to their existing custom; that believers shall stand together against wrongdoers among them and not make separate peace; that 'to the Jew who follows us belong help and equality'; that the Jews shall contribute to the cost of war while fighting alongside the believers; that 'the Jews of the B. 'Awf are one community with the believers (the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs)', with the same applying to Jewish groups linked to other named clans; that the parties shall help one another against anyone who attacks Yathrib; that Yathrib shall be a sanctuary for the people of the document; that Quraysh and their helpers shall not be given protection; and that disputes shall be referred 'to God and to Muhammad'. Guillaume notes that the single occurrence of the word 'Medina' in one clause may be a later interpolation, since the town is otherwise called Yathrib throughout.

Most modern scholars regard the text as early and substantially authentic. Lecker describes it as 'widely acknowledged as authentic and as dating back to the time of the Prophet', and judges Ignaz Goldziher's general scepticism about such documents 'too sweeping'. Donner reports a consensus, including among scholars generally sceptical of late literary sources, that it is probably a fairly accurate transcription of an early document, because in form and content it seems archaic and does not conform to later idealizing views.

Scholars disagree about its unity and date. Serjeant divided it into eight distinct documents issued at different times. Lecker argues that it is a unified document with two clearly defined parts: a treaty among the believers (the Emigrants and Helpers) and a non-belligerency treaty with some of the Jews, drawn up shortly after the Hijra, when the main Jewish clans were still the dominant political and military power in Medina. Hamidullah regarded the two parts as one complete whole of the same authorship, while suggesting that the code for the Jews may have been added after the Battle of Badr.

The position of the Jewish groups in the document is also debated. Lecker argues that the main Jewish tribes, the Nadir, Qurayza, and Qaynuqa', did not take part, that only one Jewish tribe of some weight (the Tha'laba ibn al-Fityawn) participated, and that the clause usually read as making the Jews of B. 'Awf 'one community (umma) with the believers' should be emended to grant them security (amana) from the believers. Donner reads the same clauses as evidence that some of Medina's Jews made an agreement with Muhammad in which they were recognized as part of the community of Believers. He notes that the absence of the three main clans raises questions, listing without deciding among several explanations: that the document was drawn up late, that clauses or separate documents concerning those clans were lost or dropped, or that later tradition shaped the accounts of Muhammad's conflicts with them. He leaves these questions to future scholarship.

The modern label 'constitution' is itself contested. Hamidullah described the text as the first written constitution of a state in the world. Lecker finds the term 'constitution' 'rather disorienting', and he and other scholars prefer the neutral term Kitab or the older designation 'ahd al-umma.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes the document, its transmission, and the scholarly debate about it, attributing each reading to its holder (neutrality #1, #2). Its treatment of the Jewish groups of Yathrib is kept strictly descriptive, per neutrality #11. The document's own clauses are quoted from the primary text. The questions of which Jewish groups were parties, whether they were counted as part of the umma or granted security (the umma/amana reading), and how the document relates to the later traditional accounts of conflict with the Nadir, Qurayza, and Qaynuqa' are each attributed to named scholars (Lecker, Donner, Hamidullah, Serjeant). The editor adopts none of these readings and says nothing about the later conflicts beyond what these scholars state. The label 'constitution' is kept as the entry name because it is the most widely recognized, and the objection to it is reported.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: the text of the document was read directly in Guillaume's translation of Ibn Ishaq (pp. 231-233, including Guillaume's note on the 'Medina' interpolation). Lecker's preface and introduction (pp. ix-3) were read directly in a digitized copy for his judgments on authenticity, unity, the two-part structure, the non-participation of the main Jewish tribes, the Tha'laba ibn al-Fityawn, the umma/amana emendation, Goldziher, Serjeant, and the term 'constitution'. Donner, Muhammad and the Believers, pp. 72-73 and Appendix A (pp. 227-228) were read directly for the transmission in Ibn Ishaq and Abu Ubayd, the authenticity consensus, and his reading of the Jewish clauses. Hamidullah's essay was read directly in its 1941 form in a digitized copy, for his two-part view and the post-Badr dating of the Jewish code. These are rated high for what those passages say. Serjeant's BSOAS article was verified to exist and to divide the text into separate documents (a view Lecker's introduction also reports), but was not read line by line; rated medium. Abu Ubayd's Kitab al-Amwal was verified as the second early witness through Donner and through Lecker's critical apparatus (Amwal, no. 518), and the Nyazee translation was verified to exist, but the relevant passage was not read directly; rated medium.

Sourcing triangulates the three lenses per neutrality #8: (a) Western academic scholarship (Lecker, Donner, Serjeant); (b) classical primary texts (Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; Abu Ubayd); (c) a modern Muslim scholar (Muhammad Hamidullah). No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited (neutrality #9). Dates are given in hijri and CE.

relations.note: The text presents itself as 'a document from Muhammad the prophet', and the classical sources attribute it to him; modern scholars broadly accept it as an early document from his time in Medina, while debating whether it is one text or several.
The document regulates relations in Yathrib among the Emigrants who arrived with the emigration of 622, the Medinan Helpers, and some Jewish groups; Lecker places it shortly after the emigration.
Ibn Ishaq's biography of Muhammad, in Ibn Hisham's recension, is one of the two early works that preserve the text of the document; the other is Abu Ubayd's Kitab al-Amwal.

Jewish groups of Yathrib appear in the document as parties with defined obligations and with their own religion ('the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs'); which Jewish groups took part, and on what terms, is debated among scholars.

sources.citation: Ibn Ishaq, Muhammad. Sirat Rasul Allah, recension of Ibn Hisham. Trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad: A Translation of Ishaq's Sirat Rasul Allah. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1955, pp. 231-233, 'The Covenant between the Muslims and the Medinans and with the Jews'. The full text of the document, read directly, including the umma clause, the clauses on blood-money, the Jews' share of war costs, 'the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs', Yathrib as sanctuary, and reference of disputes to God and Muhammad, together with Guillaume's note that the one occurrence of 'Medina' is probably an interpolation. The classical-primary lens. High for what the text says.
